sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Adaptive rounding methods such as GPTQ, or equivalently Babai's nearest plane algorithm, round a real matrix to integers under a quadratic metric. They process the entries in a fixed order, one at a time, propagating each rounding error to the entries not yet processed through a triangular feedback matrix. We study the two-sided version of this task, in which fixed nonsingular basis matrices act on both the left and the right of the residual; the familiar one-sided case is the special case of an identity right basis. Vectorizing the matrix turns the two-sided objective into a quadratic metric whose Gram matrix is a Kronecker product, so the one-dimensional algorithm applies verbatim, but takes quartic time in the matrix dimension. We present GPTQ-2D, which produces the identical rounded matrix in cubic time. It rounds the entries anti-diagonal by anti-diagonal; entries on the same anti-diagonal are independent and are rounded in parallel.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Adaptive rounding methods, such as GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023) or equivalently Babais nearest plane algorithm (Babai, 1986), round real matrix Rmn to an integer matrix Zmn under quadratic (squared) metric. In the one-sided case the metric for fixed nonsingular basis matrix Rmm. These methods do not is A(Z X)2 exactly minimize that objective; they greedily process the entries in fixed order, one at time, rounding each entry to the nearest integer given the entries already rounded. After an entry is rounded, its rounding error is propagated to the not-yet-processed entries through triangular feedback matrix obtained from an O(m3) factorization of the inverse of the Gram matrix. Because this one-sided metric couples only the entries within each column, the columns are then rounded independently in an O(m2n) sweep. The total work is O(m2 max(m, n)), cubic in the dimension for square matrix. This paper studies two-sided version, adding second fixed nonsingular basis matrix Rnn on the right, so that the metric becomes A(Z X)B2 = (B A)(vec(Z) vec(X))2, (1) where the second form uses the identity vec(A(Z X)B) = (B A) vec(Z X) with denoting the Kronecker product and vec() denoting the vectorization operator.1 one1. We use column-major vectorization: the entry Xij of an matrix becomes the (cid:0)(j 1)m + i(cid:1)-th entry of vec(X) Rmn. 1 dimensional adaptive rounding algorithm therefore applies to the mn vectorized coordinates. Now the right basis couples the columns too, so they no longer decouple, and direct sweep over all mn coordinates costs O(m2n2), quartic for square matrix. The Kronecker structure offers shortcut. rounding error at entry (i, j) contributes rank-one update supported only on the lower-right rectangle anchored at (i, j) (rows i, columns j), so entries on the same anti-diagonal are independent and can be rounded in parallel. Our algorithm, which we call GPTQ-2D, exploits this: rather than applying each errors rank-one update densely over its rectangle, it maintains the corrected matrix together with buffer of accumulated feedback and pushes each error only along its own row and column as soon as it is produced. The rest of the rectangle is filled in lazily by the pushes of later entries. This reproduces the exact same rounding trajectory in only O(mn max(m, n)) sweep work, versus quartic for the direct sweep. With the one-time O((max(m, n))3) Gram factorization shared by both approaches, GPTQ-2D runs in O((max(m, n))3) work in total, cubic for square matrices, with rounding sweep of + 1 parallel stages. GPTQ-2D extends GPTQ rather than competing with it. One-sided adaptive rounding is the special case = I. The question is what the extension costs. Reaching the same two-sided trajectory by vectorizing and sweeping costs O(m2n2), factor Θ(min(m, n)) more than the O(mn max(m, n)) sweep of GPTQ-2D. Removing that factor is what brings the two-sided problem down to the cost of the one-sided one: for both GPTQ and GPTQ-2D run in O(m3) work in total. Contributions. We recast two-sided matrix rounding as vector rounding under Kronecker metric, and show that the resulting feedback is rank-one and separable, so entries on shared anti-diagonal are independent. Building on that independence, we reduce the rounding sweep from the O(m2n2) of dense realization to O(mn max(m, n)). The resulting algorithm reproduces the exact one-dimensional adaptive rounding trajectory in O((max(m, n))3) work, which for matches the asymptotic cost of one-sided GPTQ on the same matrix. We prove the exact equivalence (Theorem 2) and describe blocked, GPTQ-style implementation that turns the feedback into few band-like matrix products (Section 4.3).

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Adaptive rounding via second-order information. Pruning and quantization guided by second-order information originate with Optimal Brain Surgeon (Hassibi et al., 1993), which ranks weights by inverse-Hessian saliencies and applies closed-form error-feedback update to the remaining weights. Optimal Brain Compression (Frantar & Alistarh, 2022) ports this exact one-at-a-time scheme to the layer-wise post-training objective whose per-row Hessian is the input second moment. GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023) fixes single column order shared across all rows. This lets the inverse Hessian be precomputed once as Cholesky factor, which reduces the cost from quartic to cubic for square layer and enables LLM-scale quantization. QuIP (Chee et al., 2023) recasts this triangular error feedback as LDLQ and proves it is equivalent to GPTQ. All of these methods are one-sided : single Gram matrix acts on one side of the weight matrix. 2 Lattice and nearest-plane view. Rounding under quadratic metric is exactly sweep of Babais nearest plane algorithm for the closest vector problem on the lattice induced by the metric (Babai, 1986). This connection was made precise for GPTQ by Chen et al. (2026) and Birnick (2026): GPTQs column-sequential rounding with Cholesky error feedback coincides with Babais projection sweep. In this view Kronecker Gram defines tensorproduct lattice whose Cholesky factor is the Kronecker product of the per-axis Cholesky factors, and the nearest plane on each axis is the classical primitive. The lattice view also provides an error bound for GPTQ. However, it makes no global-optimality claim. Computing an exact closest lattice point is NP-hard in general (Dinur et al., 2003). Two-sided and Kronecker-factored rounding. Closest to our setting is YAQA (Tseng et al., 2026), which rounds under Kronecker-factored Hessian by generalizing the LDLQ fixed-point iteration to left and right factor. Exploiting the Kronecker structure, it bounds the number of sweeps by at most + 1, and its reference implementation already sweeps the block anti-diagonals of the weight matrix. Each sweep applies the feedback as dense matrix products, so the iteration amounts to O(mn(max(m, n))2) work, quartic for square matrix. Up to the direction of the sweep, the two compute the same rounding: YAQA rounds in reverse order, from the last row and column, where GPTQ-2D rounds forward. GPTQ-2D computes it in O(mn max(m, n)) sweep work, cubic for square matrix, so it can be dropped in as YAQAs rounding step, leaving its Kronecker-factored Hessian sketch untouched.

Such memorybound updates are far slower than dense matrix products on parallel hardware. GPTQ owes its practical speed to lazy block updates (Frantar et al., 2023): cheap updates within block, then one dense matrix product that flushes the blocks accumulated error to all remaining coordinates. We port this idea to the anti-diagonal sweep. We process the sweep in blocks of consecutive anti-diagonals, keeping single global buffer = LE across blocks (Algorithm 4). Within block, we run Algorithm 3 with the fold and both pushes clipped at the block boundary, so every in-block update touches only the blocks anti-diagonals. Index ranges outside the matrix bounds are skipped. After the block, two band-like matrix products deliver the remaining feedback to all later entries: down flush of the band of through along the matrix columns, and right flush of the blocks anti-diagonal band of through along the matrix rows. The down flush does double duty: the product it adds to later entry Yij is exactly the part of the fold deferred past the block boundary, so the same product also completes the buffer = LE below the block, at no extra matrix product. This is GPTQs lazy block update on anti-diagonals: many small updates collapse into two band-like matrix products per block. Since the w-wide windows of and shift with the receiving row or column, each flush runs efficiently as batched matrix-vector multiplication with overlapping windows. Every feedback contribution of Algorithm 3, from one rounded entry to one later entry, is applied exactly once, either by clipped push inside the block or by flush; the buffer = LE is maintained by the clipped fold within the block and completed for the later entries by the down flush, and all feedback from block lands before the next block starts. Algorithm 4 therefore produces the same as Algorithm 3. sections.title: 5 Padded Skew Layout
sections.content: The blocked sweep of Section 4.3 touches three different access patterns: an anti-diagonal Is, matrix column Y:,j, and matrix row Yi,:. In an array-level framework (e.g., PyTorch) an update is efficient only when the entries it touches form slice with fixed stride and fixed length; otherwise it degenerates into gather. Anti-diagonals are not such slices in either the row-major or the column-major layout, so we store the working matrices in layout in which all three patterns are. This layout is property of the framework rather than of the algorithm: kernel-level implementation can keep the natural layout and mask the out-of-range lanes of each anti-diagonal instead, in which case none of the padding below is needed. The construction. We store , Z, C, and in padded array of + 1 rows with common row stride = 2m + 2 (Figure 2). Entry (i, j) is placed in row = + at intra-row position 1 + j. Since = + is constant along an anti-diagonal while the intra-row position increases with j, each anti-diagonal Is is contiguous segment of one row, with its columns in the same left-to-right order as in the matrix. The three views. The same cells then serve the other two access patterns at fixed strides. Stepping down one matrix row within fixed matrix column advances by one and leaves the intra-row position unchanged, so matrix column Y:,j is vertical stride-r line; this is the view used by the downward push and by the down flush. Stepping right one matrix column within fixed matrix row advances both and the intra-row position by one, so matrix row Yi,: is diagonal stride-(r+1) line; this is the view used by the rightward push and by the right flush. Every access of the sweep is therefore slice with fixed stride and fixed length. 11 s=2 s=3 s=4 s=5 s=6 s=7 X11 X21 X12 X31 X22 X32 X23 X14 X33 X24 X34 block w=2 anti-diagonal Is: contiguous row (round) matrix column Y:,j : stride (push down, flush) matrix row Yi,:: stride r+1 (push right, flush) block of anti-diagonals (flushed together) Figure 2: The padded skew array, for 3 4 example (rows = anti-diagonals; row stride = 2m + 2 = 8). The cells are positions that an anti-diagonal leaves empty because it has fewer than entries. The cells at the upper left and lower right are where the two ends of stride-(r+1) row line overhang. row line can overhang by up to 1 positions at either end, so each row reserves 1 positions on each side of the band, giving the row stride = 2(m 1) + = 2m + 2. Neither kind is ever read as data, since Algorithm 4 skips index ranges outside the matrix bounds, but both are allocated: buffer occupies (m + 1)(2m + 2) cells to hold mn entries of data. That is Θ((max(m, n))2), so the overhead is mild for square matrices and grows with the aspect ratio. sections.title: 6 Applications and Discussion
sections.content: The formulation separates two questions that applications often conflate. The first is algorithmic. Given two-sided quadratic objective A(Z X)B2 F, how does one efficiently compute the fixed-order rounding trajectory induced by its Kronecker metric? This paper answers that with an exact algorithm whose rounding sweep takes O(mn max(m, n)) work, factor Θ(min(m, n)) below the vectorized sweep and, for n, the same total order as one-sided GPTQ on the same matrix  (Table 1)  . The second is about modeling. How should and be chosen in given application? That question is separate. In neural network quantization, for instance, and may come from factors of Kronecker Hessian approximations. This paper does not address that estimation problem. The method should be read as work-efficient way to carry out given Kronecker-factored rounding, not as new rounding rule. 12 There are two caveats. First, the equivalence guarantee assumes the basis matrices and B, hence the feedback factors and , are fixed throughout the sweep; if they adapt to intermediate rounding decisions, for instance through data-dependent scaling, exact equivalence to the fixed vectorized procedure need not hold. Second, GPTQ-2D computes fixed-order trajectory and makes no global-optimality claim; this is inherited from onedimensional adaptive rounding, and in particular from GPTQ, rather than introduced by the two-sided setting. Computing an exact closest rounding is NP-hard in general.
